title: Context trimming
point: Send the model only the tokens it needs: summarise long observations, cap retrieval, drop stale history and cap output, which cuts both cost and latency.
definition: Context trimming reduces the tokens sent and generated on each call. It summarises long tool observations, caps retrieved passages, drops history that no longer matters and limits output length.

objective.text: Given a growing agent context, choose what to summarise, cap or drop, compute the per-call saving, and name the golden-set check that shows nothing important was lost.

misconceptions.claim: More context always gives better answers, so it is worth paying for.
misconceptions.correction: Long raw tool output and stale turns often bury the facts that matter. Trimmed context is cheaper, faster and frequently at least as accurate, which the golden set should confirm.

misconceptions.claim: Trimming only matters for input tokens.
misconceptions.correction: Output tokens usually cost several times more than input and are generated one at a time. Capping output length cuts both cost and latency.

l1: Each loop step usually appends a full tool observation, so context grows with every step. Summarise long observations to the facts the next step needs.
Cap retrieved tokens, for example to the top few passages. Drop history that no longer affects the decision, and cap output length with a maximum and a terse format.
Fewer tokens also cut latency. The model processes fewer input tokens and generates fewer output tokens, so each step finishes sooner.
l2: At step 8, an agent carries 30,000 tokens of history, mostly raw tool output. At an illustrative $2 per million input tokens, that call's input costs $0.06.
Summarise each observation to about 300 tokens and keep only the last three turns verbatim. The context falls to 9,000 tokens, and the input for that call costs $0.018.
Capping output from 2,000 to 800 tokens, at an illustrative $10 per million, cuts output cost from $0.02 to $0.008 per call.
l3: The risk is dropping a fact that a later step needs. Keep an ID for each full observation, and give the agent a tool that fetches it back on demand.

Run the golden set with and without trimming, and compare task success as well as tokens. A trim that saves 60 per cent of input tokens is still a bad trade if it costs more task success than the business allows.
Output caps need care too. A cap that truncates a structured verdict mid-field causes a parse failure and a retry, which costs more than the tokens it saved.
